To hiss means to make a sharp, continuous "sssss" sound — the kind of sound the letter S makes when you stretch it out. It is a high, thin, rushing sound produced when air or gas is forced through a very narrow space.

Think of a snake coiled on the ground, sensing danger. It opens its mouth and pushes air out fast through a tiny gap — and out comes that unmistakable, chilling ssssss. That is the definitive image of hissing.

This is important, because hissing is not just something snakes do. Many things — living and non-living — can hiss.

Animals hiss, especially when frightened or angry. A cat backs itself into a corner and hisses at a dog. A goose hisses at someone who gets too close to its nest. In every case, the animal is pushing air sharply out to make that warning sound.

Machines and gases hiss constantly in everyday life. Steam hisses out of a kettle spout. Air hisses from a punctured tire. A gas pipe with a small leak hisses quietly. A pressure cooker hisses as it releases steam. The common thread is always the same: gas or air escaping or moving through a tight space.

Wet things hitting intense heat also hiss. When you drop a piece of meat into a very hot pan, or when water touches a red-hot surface, you hear that immediate, explosive hissing sizzle. This is the same sound — gas (steam) being released rapidly.

Moving objects can hiss too, when they cut through the air fast enough. An arrow hissed through the air. A bullet hissed past his ear. A car hisses along a wet road. Here, it describes the sharp, sliding sound of something slicing through a medium at speed.

Humans hiss in two distinct ways, and it is worth understanding both clearly.

First, to show disapproval. When an audience hisses at a performer, a speaker, or a character in a play, they are deliberately making that "sss" sound as a sign of contempt or rejection. It is the opposite of applause. Historically, audiences hissed at actors they disliked. Even today, if a politician says something the crowd finds disgraceful, people might hiss. It is a way of using the snake's warning sound to say: we do not accept you.

Second, as a way of speaking. When a person is angry, trying to be threatening, or wants to say something intense without raising their voice loudly, they speak in a way that sounds like a hiss — sharp, pressurized, forced through tightened lips and teeth.

For example: "Don't you ever do that again," she hissed.

In this use, "hiss" replaces the word "said." It tells you not just that words were spoken, but how they were spoken — with a cold, controlled, dangerous intensity. It often suggests that the speaker is suppressing fury rather than exploding with it, which makes it feel more threatening, not less. Writers love this word because it does two jobs at once: it delivers the dialogue and paints the emotion.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

Hissing, in almost every context, carries a mood. It is not a friendly or neutral sound. Whether it is a snake, a crowd, or an angry person — hissing signals warning, threat, danger, contempt, or anger. Even when a machine hisses, the sound often makes people alert or uneasy, because the association is so deep.

When you read or hear that something "hissed," your instinct is to pay attention. Something tense is happening.

Here is a summary of every way the verb "hiss" is used, illustrated with examples:

To produce a "sss" sound naturally:
The snake hissed and coiled tighter. The radiator hissed all night. Steam hissed from the pipe.

To move with that sound:
The train hissed into the station. The arrow hissed through the air.

To show disapproval (as a crowd):
The audience hissed when the villain walked on stage. The crowd hissed and jeered.

To speak in a sharp, intense, angry whisper:
"Get out of my house," he hissed. She grabbed his arm and hissed, "Not another word."

In short: to hiss is to make — or to move with, or to speak with — that sharp, sustained, sibilant ssss sound. It almost always carries a sense of pressure, warning, or anger, whether the source is alive or mechanical.
